title: Gifts asked for
hookLine: the gift of Sikhi, of hair, of discipline, discernment, trust and faith

lines: A WISH LIST SAYS WHO YOU ARE.
cards: Read a child's birthday wish list and you learn a lot about the child. Read a grown-up's and you learn even more. Usually the list is made of things: a phone, a car, a trip, a bigger kitchen.
The Ardas has a wish list too, and it's made of things you can't buy, wrap or hold. Each item ends with the same word, daan, a gift, so that said aloud it has a rhythm, like a steady drumbeat.
Six of them come before the last and greatest.

teach.b: A little further on, the community asks: sikhaan noon sikhee daan, kes daan, rahit daan, bibek daan, visaah daan, bharosaa daan. To the Sikhs, give the gift of Sikhi, of kes, of rahit, of bibek, of visaah, of bharosaa.
Daan is a gift, the kind given freely, not earned. Take them in turn.

teach.h: SIKHI, KES, RAHIT: THE PATH ITSELF.
teach.b: Sikhee daan: the gift of Sikhi itself, the path, the life of a learner. Even being a Sikh is treated as a gift to receive, not an achievement. Kes daan: the gift of uncut hair, which Sikhs keep as the Guru's form.
The martyrs kept it to the last breath; here it's asked for as something given. Rahit daan: the gift of discipline, the Sikh way of life kept day after day.
Bibek daan: the gift of discernment, telling right from wrong, true from false, especially when it's hard to see.

Visaah daan and bharosaa daan: the gift of trust and the gift of faith. They sound alike, and they overlap. One way Sikhs gloss them: visaah as trusting, bharosaa as the confidence to lean your whole weight on God.
Both are asked for, side by side, as if one weren't enough. None of these is about circumstances. The Ardas doesn't ask here for an easier life.
It asks for the inner equipment to live any life well: discipline, discernment, trust.
Ask for faith, the Ardas suggests, and you're asking for something no situation can take.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs ask for a string of gifts: Sikhi, kes, rahit, bibek, visaah and bharosaa, each ending in daan, before the greatest gift of all.

o: strict discipline in daily Sikh life
a quiet trust that leans on God

games.q: gifts asked for — tap the pairs.

s: in the Ardas, even Sikhi itself is asked for as a gift
sikhee daan: the path is received, not achieved.
the gifts in this list are mostly about easier circumstances
they're the inner equipment to live any life well.
visaah and bharosaa are both asked for, side by side
trust and faith, as if one weren't enough.

games.q: you have a hard decision to make today, and you can't tell which way is right. which gift in the Ardas fits?
games.why: bibek is discernment: telling right from wrong, true from false, especially when it's hard to see.

practice: Let the six pass slowly through your mind: the path, the form, discipline, discernment, trust, faith, and notice which one you feel the lack of right now; maybe bibek for a decision, bharosaa for a fear, rahit for a habit that's slipped.
If you pray, ask for it in the Ardas's own word, daan, a gift; if you don't, hold it as a hope for the day.

wordCard.voice: Bibek, discernment: one of six daan, alongside Sikhi, kes, rahit, visaah, bharosaa, none of them things you can buy.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bibek, discernment; bibek daan, the gift of telling true from false.

carryVoice: Your line: ask for faith. Nothing on this list can be bought or wrapped. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Ardas, as set out in the Sikh Rehat Maryada (SGPC)
